introduction_markdown: Time allowed: two and a half hours. Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour and Section II in 1 1/2 hours; you are advised to divide your time accordingly. In Section II answer EITHER a, b and c OR d, e and f of each question. For your guidance the approximate mark for each part of a question is indicated in brackets. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation of your answers. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Where necessary, assume: the acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the earth, $g = 10\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$; the speed of light in air, $c = 3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the charge on an electron, $e = 1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}$. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown: **Answer EITHER 8 a, b and c OR 8 d, e and f.**
incertitudes: Le sujet n'imprime pas de total par question : les totaux (`points` de l'exercice) sont la somme des points imprimés bloc par bloc (Section I : 6+4+8+6+9+7 = 40 ; Section II : 20 par question, soit 100 au total).

Les schémas, diagrammes et graphes demandés à l'élève (tracé de graphe, diagramme de rayons, champ électrique ou magnétique, tension d'entrée et de sortie, schéma de montage) ne sont pas produits comme figures du corrigé : ils sont décrits dans le corrigé (axes, points clés, forme).

Question 8(b)(ii) et 8(e)(ii) : les graphes sont à tracer par l'élève ; le corrigé donne les échelles conseillées, les points à placer et l'allure de la courbe (montée puis palier à 95 degrés ; décroissance exponentielle du taux de comptage).

Question 8(e) : le sujet annonce une durée de 200 heures mais le tableau s'arrête à 100 h ; recopié tel quel. La période est lue sur le graphe : 1800 -> 900 en 40 h puis 900 -> 450 en 40 h, soit 40 h (une lecture entre 38 h et 43 h est acceptable car les points mesurés sont dispersés : 1200 à 20 h contre 1273 attendu).

Question 8(b)(iv) : le sujet demande une raison pour laquelle le point d'ébullition peut différer de la valeur standard ; deux raisons classiques sont données (impuretés, pression différente de la pression atmosphérique normale), une seule est exigée.

Question 8(f) : le noyau $^{56}_{22}X$ et le produit Y sont hypothétiques (le sujet ne nomme pas l'élément) ; la conservation du nombre de masse et du numéro atomique donne Y = $^{52}_{21}Y$ quel que soit l'ordre des émissions alpha et bêta.
Question 8(a)(iv) : la longueur du fil de mercure est supposée varier linéairement avec la température entre les deux points fixes (5 cm à 0 degré, 45 cm à 100 degrés).

questions.enonce_markdown:
When an un-calibrated liquid-in-glass thermometer is placed in pure melting ice, the length of the mercury thread is $5\,\mathrm{cm}$. When it is placed in steam from boiling water under standard atmospheric pressure, the length of the thread is $45\,\mathrm{cm}$.

(i) Define thermometric property. *[2 marks]*

(ii) State the thermometric property of the liquid-in-glass thermometer. *[1 mark]*

(iii) What is the name given to the mercury level on the thermometer when it is placed in steam? *[1 mark]*

(iv) Calculate the temperature for which the length of the thread will be $25\,\mathrm{cm}$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) A **thermometric property** is a **physical property of a substance that changes continuously (and measurably) with temperature**, and which is used to measure temperature: for example the length of a liquid column, the resistance of a wire or the pressure of a gas at constant volume.

(ii) The **length of the liquid (mercury) thread** (or column) in the glass tube.

(iii) The **upper fixed point** (the steam point, $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

(iv) The lower fixed point (ice) is $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $5\,\mathrm{cm}$ and the upper fixed point (steam) is $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ at $45\,\mathrm{cm}$. The length changes uniformly with temperature, so

$\theta = \dfrac{l_\theta - l_0}{l_{100} - l_0} \times 100 = \dfrac{25 - 5}{45 - 5} \times 100 = \dfrac{20}{40} \times 100 = 50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$

**The temperature is $50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
In an experiment to determine the boiling point of a liquid, the temperature of the liquid, $\theta$, and the corresponding times, $t$, were recorded as the liquid was heated for a period of $20\,\mathrm{minutes}$. The results obtained are shown on the table below.

| $\theta/^\circ\mathrm{C}$ | 27 | 65 | 83 | 95 | 95 | 95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $t/\mathrm{min}$ | 0 | 4 | 8 | 12 | 16 | 20 |

(i) Define boiling point. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Plot a graph of temperature, $\theta$, on the y-axis against time, $t$, on the x-axis. *[5 marks]*

(iii) Determine the boiling point of the liquid from your graph. *[2 marks]*

(iv) Give one reason why the boiling point can be different from the standard value. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The **boiling point** is the **constant temperature at which a liquid boils**, that is, the temperature at which its saturated vapour pressure equals the external (atmospheric) pressure.

(ii) **Graph (to be drawn):** x-axis: time $t/\mathrm{min}$ from 0 to 20 (for example $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $2\,\mathrm{min}$); y-axis: temperature $\theta/^\circ\mathrm{C}$ from 20 to 100 (for example $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$). Label both axes with their units, use a suitable scale that fills the page, and plot the six points with small crosses:

| $t/\mathrm{min}$ | 0 | 4 | 8 | 12 | 16 | 20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\theta/^\circ\mathrm{C}$ | 27 | 65 | 83 | 95 | 95 | 95 |

Join them with a **smooth curve**: the temperature rises quickly at first, then more slowly (slope decreasing: 38, 18 then 12 degrees in 4 minutes), and then the curve becomes a **horizontal straight line (plateau) at $95\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$** from about 12 minutes to 20 minutes.

(iii) The temperature stops rising and stays constant on the plateau: **boiling point $= 95\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$**.

(iv) Any one of: the liquid contains **dissolved impurities**, which raise the boiling point; or the **external pressure** is different from standard atmospheric pressure (a lower pressure, for example at high altitude, lowers the boiling point and a higher pressure raises it).

questions.enonce_markdown:
An electric heater rated $900\,\mathrm{W}$ is used to heat $2\,\mathrm{kg}$ of water at $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in $5$ minutes. Calculate:

(i) the quantity of heat energy supplied to the water during this time. *[3 marks]*

(ii) the change in temperature of the water given that the specific heat capacity of water is $4200\,\mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,^\circ C^{-1}}$. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Energy supplied = power $\times$ time, with $t = 5 \times 60 = 300\,\mathrm{s}$:

$Q = Pt = 900 \times 300 = 270\,000\,\mathrm{J}$

**$Q = 2.7\times10^{5}\,\mathrm{J}$ (270 kJ).**

(ii) $Q = mc\,\Delta\theta$, so

$\Delta\theta = \dfrac{Q}{mc} = \dfrac{270\,000}{2 \times 4200} = \dfrac{270\,000}{8400} = 32.1\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$

**The temperature rises by about $32\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$** (from $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to about $62\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), assuming that all the energy goes into the water.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In an experiment to determine the count rate of a radioactive substance, a student records a count of $20\,\mathrm{counts\ per\ second}$ and $18\,\mathrm{counts\ per\ second}$ respectively before and after the experiment when there was no actual source present in front of the GM tube. When a radioactive carbon was placed in front of the GM tube, a count rate of $239\,\mathrm{counts\ per\ second}$ was recorded.

(i) Define background radiation. *[1 mark]*

(ii) State one source of background radiation. *[1 mark]*

(iii) Calculate the background count rate for this experiment. *[1 mark]*

(iv) Calculate the actual count rate of the radioactive carbon. *[2 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Background radiation** is the **ionising radiation that is always present in the environment**, coming from natural sources (and a little from man-made sources), and which is detected by a GM tube even when no radioactive source is nearby.

(ii) Any one of: **cosmic rays** from space; **radon gas** from the ground; **rocks and soil** (uranium, thorium); building materials; food and water; medical X-rays; fallout from nuclear tests.

(iii) The background count rate is the **mean** of the two readings taken before and after the experiment:

$\dfrac{20 + 18}{2} = 19\ \text{counts per second}$

(iv) Actual count rate = measured count rate $-$ background count rate:

$239 - 19 = 220\ \text{counts per second}$

**The actual count rate of the radioactive carbon is $220\ \mathrm{counts\ s^{-1}}$.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
In an experiment to determine the half-life of a radioactive substance, the count rates of the substance and the corresponding times were recorded as the substance decays for a period of $200\,\mathrm{hours}$. The results obtained are shown on the table below.

| Count rate / $\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$ | 1800 | 1200 | 900 | 640 | 450 | 340 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Time / hrs | 0 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 80 | 100 |

(i) Define half-life. *[1 mark]*

(ii) Plot a graph of count rate on the y-axis against time on the x-axis. *[5 marks]*

(iii) Use the graph to determine the half-life of the substance. *[2 marks]*

(iv) Give one reason why some of the plotted points do not fall on the line. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The **half-life** is the **time taken for the count rate (activity) of a radioactive substance, or equivalently the number of undecayed nuclei, to fall to half of its initial value**.

(ii) **Graph (to be drawn):** x-axis: time / hrs from 0 to 100 (for example $2\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $20\,\mathrm{h}$); y-axis: count rate / $\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$ from 0 to 1800 (for example $1\,\mathrm{cm}$ for $200\,\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$). Label the axes with units, plot the points $(0,\,1800)$, $(20,\,1200)$, $(40,\,900)$, $(60,\,640)$, $(80,\,450)$, $(100,\,340)$ and draw a **smooth decreasing curve** (exponential decay) through, or close to, the points: steep at first, then flatter, never touching the time axis.

(iii) Initial count rate $= 1800\,\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$, so half of it is $\dfrac{1800}{2} = 900\,\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$. On the curve, $900\,\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$ is reached at $t = 40\,\mathrm{h}$ (draw the dotted lines on the graph).

Check: from $900$ to $450\,\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}$ the time is $80 - 40 = 40\,\mathrm{h}$.

**The half-life is about $40\,\mathrm{hours}$.**

(iv) Radioactive decay is a **random process**: the number of nuclei disintegrating in each interval fluctuates (statistical variation), so the measured counts scatter around the smooth curve. (Another acceptable reason: the readings include background radiation or counting errors.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
An unstable radioactive substance $^{56}_{22}X$ decays to a stable substance Y by emitting an alpha and a beta particle.

(i) Write the equation for the decay process with the correct symbols for the alpha and beta particles. *[2 marks]*

(ii) Determine the mass number and the proton number of the substance Y. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
An **alpha particle** is a helium nucleus, $^{4}_{2}\alpha$ (or $^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$): it removes 4 from the mass number and 2 from the proton number. A **beta particle** is a fast electron, $^{0}_{-1}\beta$ (or $^{0}_{-1}e$): it leaves the mass number unchanged and **adds 1** to the proton number (a neutron becomes a proton).

(i) The decay equation is:

$$
^{56}_{22}X \;\longrightarrow\; ^{52}_{21}Y \;+\; ^{4}_{2}\alpha \;+\; ^{0}_{-1}\beta
$$

(ii) Mass number of Y: $A = 56 - 4 - 0 = 52$.

Proton number of Y: $Z = 22 - 2 + 1 = 21$.

Check: mass numbers $52 + 4 + 0 = 56$; proton numbers $21 + 2 - 1 = 22$, both are conserved.

**Y has mass number $52$ and proton number $21$, that is $^{52}_{21}Y$.**
